entry.title: Microsoft Patches High-Severity Flaw in Authenticator for Android
entry.content:
Links: cybersecuritynews.com | source

Microsoft has patched a high-severity local elevation-of-privilege vulnerability (CVE-2026-80097) in the Microsoft Authenticator app for Android. Discovered by Enclave researchers, the flaw allowed malicious local applications with no declared permissions to spoof trusted Microsoft apps and request delegated account access tokens without user interaction.

The vulnerability stemmed from improper authentication within the app's broker component, specifically an exported Android activity that failed to verify whether the calling application matched the claimed identity in the request. By passing signature checks associated with legitimately installed apps like Microsoft Teams, unauthorized applications could access sensitive resources including mailboxes, OneDrive files, and SharePoint content. Microsoft addressed the flaw in Authenticator version 6.2606.4246.

After successfully writing custom Haskell code to send emails via SMTP, he discovered that the primary challenges lie outside basic protocol implementation.

While technical hurdles like setting up DNS records and TLS are manageable, delivering messages reliably across all major providers requires navigating complex, opaque spam filters and IP address block blacklists. Because some inbox providers penalize entire IP blocks based on third-party spam activity, senders must often acquire dedicated infrastructure and high-volume sending profiles, which explains the real-world costs of email delivery.

entry.title: IETF Draft Defines MoLE Protocols for Unlinkable Endorsements
entry.content:
Links: datatracker.ietf.org | discussion

An Internet-Draft authored by contributors from Google, Mozilla, and Cloudflare outlines the protocols that instantiate the Moderation of unLinkable Endorsements (MoLE) architecture. The specification details two endorsement protocols—Issuer-Hiding Anonymous Token (IHAT) and Longfellow—which enable clients to prove they hold a trusted endorsement without revealing the specific anchor.

Additionally, the document defines three credential protocols: Anonymous Credit Tokens (ACT), Privacy Pass with a Reverse Flow, and Budget Privacy Pass. These mechanisms allow moderators to issue, verify, and update per-client state while preventing presentation linkage, alongside provisions for key rotation, discovery, and security considerations.

entry.title: Security Risks of the POSIX wordexp(3) Function Examined
entry.content:
Links: yossarian.net | discussion

The POSIX wordexp(3) C API, commonly recommended for shell-style expansions such as tilde expansion, presents significant security risks when handling untrusted inputs because it enables command expansion by default. Developers must explicitly pass the WRDE_NOCMD flag to disable this behavior, though this mitigation is frequently insufficient.

Various libc implementations, including musl and macOS libc, delegate expansion directly to the underlying system shell after performing perfunctory scanning. Bypasses in these implementations demonstrate that they can fail to catch valid command substitution patterns, making wordexp(3) unsafe for processing untrusted data.

entry.title: Bitflux Compares DiskArray and AVL Tree Performance in Memory Is Slow, Disk Is Fast Part 3
entry.content:
Links: bitflux.ai | discussion

In the third installment of its performance analysis series, Bitflux challenges traditional computer science assumptions by demonstrating that a disk-based data structure, DiskArray, can outperform an in-RAM AVL binary tree at scale. Running on a 24-core Xeon server with NVMe drives, the analysis compares sorted arrays, linked lists, AVL trees, and DiskArray across search, retrieval, insertion, and deletion operations.

While an AVL tree holds a performance advantage when data fits within CPU cache limits, DiskArray scales significantly better once data moves into main memory, eventually surpassing the in-RAM tree at 16 million nodes and continuing up to 64 billion nodes before the AVL tree runs out of RAM. The breakdown examines how contiguous data layouts and optimized disk block transfers allow DiskArray to efficiently handle heavy workloads despite moving more raw bytes overall.

Initially highlighted in Node.js under the name Node2Shell, the flaw allows unauthenticated remote attackers to corrupt memory, cause crashes, leak sensitive data, or execute arbitrary code via crafted Brotli-compressed data streams.

entry.title: FoxIO Discloses QPACK Amplification Attacks Affecting Multiple HTTP/3 Servers
entry.content:
Links: foxio.io | discussion | hacker news

Security research firm FoxIO has disclosed a class of vulnerabilities dubbed "Header Accordions" affecting QPACK, the header compression protocol used by HTTP/3. By exploiting missing or poorly enforced decoded-header limits, an unauthenticated remote client can send carefully crafted requests that force servers to allocate exponentially more memory than the payload occupies on the wire.

Testing ten different HTTP/3 implementations revealed that seven are vulnerable to memory exhaustion or denial-of-service conditions, with amplification ratios reaching up to 4000:1 in some software. While several major libraries including quic-go, Cloudflare quiche, and lsquic have issued patches and CVE identifiers, other unpatched environments require manual mitigations or server-side restrictions.
